name: Gbaya
confidence_why: Santandrea 1976 and Tucker & Bryan 1966 both put stress on the first syllable of disyllabic words, but Struck 1918, describing a single southern-Kresh speaker, denies that the language has any word stress and treats the initial prominence as a by-product of final-vowel reduction in a three-tone language, so the placement is agreed while whether it is stress at all is not.

catalog_quote: [Struck 1918: 69] 2. Akzent. Im allgemeinen werden Stamm- und Afformativsilben mit gleichem Nachdruck gesprochen, so daß sich Haupt- oder Nebenakzent nicht unterscheiden läßt. Eine scheinbare Akzentuierung der Stammsilbe entsteht durch die weitgehende Reduktion der Auslautvokale, die übrigens in der Rede schwankt und am häufigsten da eintritt, wo Auslautvokal und Stammvokal die gleiche Tonhöhe haben, auch sonst bei tieftonigem Auslaut, am seltensten bei hochtonigem Auslaut und tieftonigem Stammvokal. Da auch die vor infigiertem *li eintretenden Flüstervokale mit wesentlich geringerem als normalem Nachdruck gesprochen werden, so täuschen einzelne Wörter, wie z. B. kèléndi »Ohrgehänge«, leicht einen auf der vorletzten Silbe liegenden Starkton vor, während eine Verstärkung des Nachdrucks tatsächlich nicht stattfindet. [p. 54 fn. 9] ... daß bei dem Fehlen des Starktons ... [Tucker & Bryan 1966: 64, snippet] 2b. Stress Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. Occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable, when the first one contains a central vowel. Stevenson records stress on the second syllable in BAGIRMI k;lá, snake, for instance. [Santandrea 1976, snippet, no page] In this case, the accent lies on the first syllable and on the enclitic or suffix, the second syllable remaining altogether unaccented.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kresh is tonal (three tone levels per Tucker & Bryan; Santandrea marks tones throughout). Word stress, per the group-level statement covering Kresh, falls on the first syllable of disyllabic words (obligatorily when the second syllable has a reduced 'semi-mute' vowel; a central vowel in the first syllable can let stress fall on the second). Santandrea's Kresh-specific fragment agrees: 'the accent lies on the first syllable and on the enclitic or suffix, the second syllable remaining altogether unaccented' when enclitics/suffixes are added.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit secondary-stress statement. Santandrea 1976 describes a second accent on the enclitic or suffix in suffixed words (stem-initial syllable + enclitic/suffix accented, stem-second syllable unaccented).
new_statements.exceptions: Tucker & Bryan: stress occasionally on the second syllable when the first contains a central vowel; the only cited example is Bagirmi (Stevenson), not Kresh. Santandrea: 'suffixes differ not only in tone, but sometimes also in stress'; his paradigm tables mark individual forms as 'stressed 2nd / unstressed 1st', so stress in inflected forms is not uniformly initial.
new_statements.domain_note: Tucker & Bryan's statement is a chapter-level generalisation for the 'Bongo-Bagirmi' languages as they delimit them (Kresh explicitly included among the languages they analysed for tone), i.e. not a Kresh-only rule; word level, disyllables. Santandrea's fragments are Kresh-specific (Kresh-Ndogo dialect), word level with enclitics/suffixes, but reached only as page-less Google Books snippets. Neither quote has a print page locator.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Santandrea 1976 describes Kresh-Ndogo (alias Gbaya-Ndogo), the prestige dialect spoken near Deim Zubeir/Raga (Glottolog gbay1289 'Kresh Ndogo', a dialect of gbay1288). Tucker & Bryan's 'KRESH' is Kresh generally within their 'Bongo-Bagirmi' chapter. Struck 1918's 'Gbaya (Dar-Fertit)' = Kresh per Glottolog. 'Gbaya' here is unrelated to the Ubangian Gbaya languages.

new_statements.translation: 2. Accent. In general, stem and affix syllables are spoken with equal force, so that a main or secondary accent cannot be distinguished. An apparent accentuation of the stem syllable arises from the far-reaching reduction of final vowels, which moreover varies in speech and occurs most often where the final vowel and the stem vowel have the same pitch, otherwise also with a low-toned final, and most rarely with a high-toned final and a low-toned stem vowel. [...] so that individual words, e.g. kèlèndì 'ear pendant', easily simulate a strong stress lying on the penultimate syllable, whereas a strengthening of force does not actually take place. (p. 69) — p. 54 fn. 9: Anticipating, it should be noted right away that given the absence of a strong stress [...] (he therefore uses the Christaller/Westermann tone notation rather than Meinhof's).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's existing statement (Tucker & Bryan 1966, Bongo-Bagirmi chapter §2b, 'Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words..') is a group-level statement covering Kresh among others and implies word stress exists, typically initial. Struck 1918, the only primary description of this variety in the list, says there is NO word stress in Gbaya/Kresh (equal force on all syllables; the impression of stem/penultimate stress is illusory), i.e. a different type, not a different placement. Santandrea 1976 (Google Books snippets already held by the project) speaks of stress on the first syllable and on enclitics/suffixes, siding with Tucker & Bryan against Struck.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language has no word stress: all syllables (stem and affix) carry equal force, and no main vs secondary accent can be told apart. Pitch ('musikalischer Ton', p. 67: low, mid, high and compound tones, 'von größter Bedeutung') is the operative prosody. What sounds like stem-syllable or penultimate stress is an artefact of final-vowel reduction and of the whispered vowels before infixed *li, not a real increase in force.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly none: 'Haupt- oder Nebenakzent [läßt sich] nicht unterscheiden' (main or secondary accent cannot be distinguished).
new_statements.exceptions: Apparent stem-syllable accent from final-vowel reduction (most frequent when final and stem vowel share a pitch, or with low-toned finals; rarest with high-toned final + low-toned stem); apparent penultimate stress in words with whispered vowels before infixed *li (kèlèndì 'ear pendant'). Both are called illusory.
new_statements.identity_note: Struck 1918 describes 'Gbaya' of Dar-Fertit as spoken by one informant, Abd el-Farâd (Gbaya name Ngadja), who grew up in 'Gbaya feriego, der ersten der beschriebenen Gbaya-Enklaven' in the Bili/Biri valley near Dem-Gudju, south of Dar-For (pp. 53, 55-56), recorded at the 'Kairo' show, Luna-Park Halensee, Berlin, summer 1911. Gbaya is the Kresh autonym; this is the southern Kresh (Naka/Ndogo area) variety = Glottolog gbay1288 Kresh-Woro [krs], not the northern Dongo variety (dong1296) and unrelated to Ubangian Gbaya. Boyeldieu 2020 is a Central Sudanic family overview in which Kresh, Dongo, Woro, Aja and Birri are set aside as 'indeterminate outsiders'; it describes no particular variety.

readall_conflicts: Struck 1918 (p. 69 '2. Akzent'; p. 54 fn. 9 'Fehlen des Starktons') states that Gbaya (southern Kresh) has no word stress at all: stem and affix syllables are pronounced with equal force, no main or secondary accent is distinguishable, and apparent stem-initial or penultimate prominence is an illusion produced by final-vowel reduction and whispered vowels; pitch (low, mid, high, compound) is the meaningful prosody. This contradicts the catalog's existing statement from Tucker & Bryan 1966 (group-level for Bongo-Bagirmi incl. Kresh: stress normally on the first syllable of disyllables, invariably when the second syllable has a semi-mute vowel, occasionally second-syllable) and the Santandrea 1976 snippets held by the project (accent on the first syllable and on the enclitic/suffix; forms annotated stressed/unstressed). The disagreement is about whether word stress exists at all, not about its position; the two later works, based on far more data, treat stress as real and typically initial, while Struck's material comes from one hour-sessions with a single informant in Berlin in 1911. Boyeldieu 2020 is silent on stress.
